term: "Sigmoid"

## Simple explanation

The sigmoid function squashes any real number into a value between zero
and one. It is often used to represent a binary model's estimated
probability, though that interpretation depends on training and calibration.

## Technical explanation

The logistic sigmoid is $\sigma(x)=1/(1+e^{-x})$. Its output approaches
zero for large negative inputs and one for large positive inputs; its
derivative is $\sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x))$. Saturation at extreme inputs can
contribute to small gradients.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Sigmoid is common in binary classification output layers and in gates of
architectures such as LSTMs. It is generally not used as the hidden
activation in deep networks when alternatives offer more favorable
optimization behavior.

## How it works

The function applies an exponential transformation and normalization to
each input. For binary classification, a model can output a logit $z$ and
apply sigmoid to obtain a score in $(0,1)$, then use a threshold to make a
class decision.

## Practical example

A binary classifier for equipment failure can transform its logit with
sigmoid to produce a score. A threshold selected on validation data
determines when the system raises an alert.

## Common misconceptions

- A sigmoid output is not automatically a well-calibrated probability.
- Applying sigmoid independently to multiple classes does not enforce that
  their scores sum to one.
